metadata.title: Compass 12-Computational thinking, socioeconomic gaps and policy implications_0

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The brief uses ICILS 2018 grade-8 (or grade-9 in some countries) task-based assessments for computer and information literacy (CIL) and computational thinking (CT), pooled across participating countries. The text reports socioeconomic gaps as differences in average test scores between high- and low-status groups and then estimates regression coefficients with country fixed effects, but it does not describe the application of ICILS sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures. Because the manuscript does not specify any weight variables (e.g., student/sampling weights) or variance estimation approach, weighting cannot be confirmed from the provided text. Analysts using ICILS microdata should apply the official ICILS complex survey weights when estimating population-representative gaps and standard errors; however, this brief’s methodological details on weights are not documented here.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this brief are CIL and CT test scores reported as scaled proficiency measures, and the text does not describe whether these are PV-based achievement scores or how PVs were handled. Because the paper does not document a plausible-values strategy (e.g., Rubin’s rules, PV averaging) and does not report a missing-data handling method, this is a reporting gap rather than a design-based non-applicability. Given that ICILS is an ILSA that typically uses PVs for cognitive achievement, the absence of explicit PV and missing-data documentation limits reproducibility and correct uncertainty quantification.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used ICILS 2018 data for grade-8 students (or grade-9 in some countries) from the set of countries that participated in both the CIL and CT components; CT was optional and was taken up by 9 of the 14 ICILS 2018 countries. Socioeconomic status was operationalized using two proxies: (1) parental tertiary education vs below tertiary education, and (2) parental professional/specialist occupation (ISCO-08 one-digit 1, 2, 3) vs other occupations. The analysis pools data across countries that administered both CIL and CT and then estimates regression models with country fixed effects; the brief does not report additional exclusions (e.g., missing covariates) or any explicit missing-data rule.

data.outcome_summary: This brief uses ICILS 2018 grade-8 (or grade-9 in some countries) data to compare socioeconomic gaps in computer and information literacy (CIL) versus computational thinking (CT). CT was an optional component and was administered in 9 of the 14 participating countries; the authors pool countries that took both CIL and CT and compute gaps as differences in average scaled test scores between high-status and low-status groups. Two socioeconomic proxies are used: parental tertiary education and parental professional/specialist occupation (ISCO-08 1–3). Across countries, students from more advantaged backgrounds score higher in both CIL and CT, with the CT gap typically larger than the CIL gap; pooled regression with country fixed effects yields an estimated CT gap of 52 points vs 45 points for CIL (education proxy) and 45 vs 40 points (occupation proxy), both statistically significant. The brief does not report ICILS plausible-values handling or missing-data procedures, and it does not document whether complex survey weights were applied, limiting interpretability of uncertainty and reproducibility.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This document is a policy brief/report that performs descriptive comparisons and pooled regression with country fixed effects rather than training or evaluating machine-learning models. As a result, there are no ML algorithms to extract, and the schema’s main_findings table for predictive ML targets is intentionally left empty. Additionally, the brief does not provide the technical details needed to extract PV and missing-data handling, nor does it report an analytic sample size.
